doc.title: Gerald Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Early jazz dates, first recordings and King Porter Stomp
summary: Wilson gives birth years for Jelly Roll, Kid Ory, King Oliver, Duke and Henderson, the first recordings, and the importance of King Porter Stomp.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: 1899 and Fletcher Henderson was born in 1898. And Jelly Roll Morton was born in 1865. Yeah, 1865. Kid Ory was born in 1886 and the trumpet player…

King Oliver, King Oliver, see, King Oliver, eighteen. So at that time, you know, these guys were already, they were listening to Buddy Bolden. That’s who Jelly Roll Morton and them were listening to and now, Jesse I don’t know about Jesse in that story, although he married a Mexican woman. He’s in a Mexican cemetery here in Los Angeles, Calvary, for years they said it was Evergreen but it’s not Evergreen he’s in Calvary. In fact, I had planned to go out to his gravesite. I could have seen him if I had gone to see him but by that time he was my favorite musician. My brother and I had his records, his early records. See, the first record was made by the Original Dixieland Jazz Band.

Then it wasn’t until three years later that they let a black make a record. Kid Ory they let make a couple of sides, a couple of sides. But as I say, King Oliver and Jelly Roll made a number together, King Porter Stomp, which by the way the reason it’s named, and King Porter Stomp was the biggest jazz number. If your band didn’t have an arrangement of King Porter Stomp, you were not in. King Porter Stomp is one hell of a composition. It’s, I plan to write it one day. If you hear, if you hear what’s-his-name arrangement, Fletcher Henderson arrangement for Benny Goodman, and you hear this great number, it’s unbelievable. I know the number ‘cause we used to play it, we used to play it, we used to play it, I played it with Gloster Current’s band. It opens with a trumpet solo, it opens with a trumpet solo, yeah. I’m telling you, it’s really something.
We only have a few minutes left.
